summary:
Visitors in Gombe State stand under two overlapping criminal regimes. Nationally, Nigeria's Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reaches all persons including tourists, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex relationship and the operation of gay organisations; the UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Gombe is one of the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into its criminal legislation by 2002, as documented in Human Rights Watch's 2004 report, which also records that Shari'a courts hold criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law. The state's Shari'a Penal Code Law 2001 was signed on 23 November 2001 and criminalises same-sex conduct by men and women on terms harsher than the federal code.

Under Gombe's 2001 statute, the sodomy offence punishes unmarried men with caning of 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajm); the lesbianism offence carries up to 50 lashes and imprisonment of up to six months. Gombe defines gross indecency in its own formulation as any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour, a formulation broad enough to reach gender non-conformity in public.

The UK Home Office note (June 2025) records that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states and criminalises same-sex acts both between men and between women. The maximum penalty for sodomy for men is death in all twelve states, and penalties for lesbianism range from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Shari'a provisions and on the attitude of the hisbah, the religious morality police operating in northern states.

Enforcement in Gombe is documented at the incident level. In October 2023 the Gombe State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps raided a gathering at Duwa Plaza along the Bauchi-Gombe Expressway that was preparing a same-sex wedding, arresting 76 people. State spokesperson Buhari Sa'ad told reporters that 59 males were detained, 21 of whom wilfully confessed to being homosexuals, and that 17 females were present, adding that the detainees would be charged to court for a crime of social vice in Gombe State.

The Guardian of 23 October 2023 independently confirmed the arrests after a tip-off about a same-sex birthday and planned marriage, with Gombe NSCDC Commandant Mohammed Muazu confirming the operation and spokesperson Buhari Saad stating that 21 of the 59 detained males were involved in gay activities while the remaining males and the 17 females were invited guests and onlookers. Officers voiced concern over the ages of participants. Two Lagos-based press accounts of the same raid establish that Gombe applies its moral-crimes layer on the ground rather than leaving it on paper.

No legal protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity exists at either level. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states, which includes Gombe.
tangentialFactors:
Gombe's sodomy provision is shared verbatim with Jigawa, Kano and Zamfara, indicating a common statutory template across several northern states rather than an isolated Gombe drafting choice. The pattern of penalties across those states runs from caning and short imprisonment for unmarried men to stoning for married men.

The federal layer and the state Shari'a layer operate simultaneously. A visitor who is Muslim in Gombe faces exposure under both the national Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and state Shari'a provisions, with the state penalties reaching further than the federal ones for conduct that is already criminal nationally.

The October 2023 arrests were made by the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, a security agency rather than the police, after a tip-off. That detail suggests detection may come through informants and private gatherings rather than only through visible conduct in public, and it widens the range of agencies a visitor may encounter.

Press coverage of the raid raised the ages of participants as a concern, and the state framed the offence as social vice. Both framings give local officials latitude to characterise ambiguous conduct as a public-morals matter.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 76 people arrested in Gombe in October 2023 were ultimately charged, convicted or released is not resolved by the sources available here; the reports establish arrest and stated intent to charge only.

Whether Shari'a sexual-offence provisions have been applied in a completed prosecution in Gombe, as opposed to being on the statute book, is not established in these sources. The heaviest penalties recorded for Gombe (stoning for married men) derive from the annotated statutory volume, not from a reported case.

Whether proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, reported nationally in September 2022, have been enacted in Gombe or federally is unsettled by the sources here. No trans-specific violence or imprisonment case from Gombe State appears in this inventory; the documented national trans cases originate elsewhere.

How Gombe authorities would house a transgender detainee, and whether any state-level protection from arbitrary arrest exists, is not sourced for this state.
